name: Light Grey
lede: Light Grey is the pale neutral that web designers know as `lightgrey`, and a plain descriptive name that the books use for mourning cloth, Vermeer's walls and overcast skies.

sections.title: A named grey in the standards
sections.body:
The swatch is #D3D3D3, the value Paterson's dictionary gives for LightGrey, one of the colors in the X11 set [1]. The same dictionary lists Gainsboro, also described as a light grey, at #DCDCDC [1]. In our library the two are a near-duplicate pair, 2.1 units apart [2].

Other systems land close by. RAL 7035, the German industrial light grey, sits near #CBD0CC on screen, and the xkcd color survey's version is #D8DCD6 [2]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files this swatch in block 264 [2]. As a screen color, all of these are approximations.

sections.title: The words around it
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary shows how many older names crowd the same pale grey. Elephant is a light grey, though sometimes a dark one [3]. Oyster white is a light grey or a greyish white, and *oyster* as a color description is first recorded in 1922 on Fowler's authority [3]. Elephant's breath is a light grey that Maerz and Paul, according to Paterson, found hard to match to an authentic original [3].

Its neighbors in our app are [[silver-grey]], [[pearl-grey]], [[dove-grey]] and [[silver]], and above it [[white]] [2].

sections.title: Light grey in use
sections.body:
Mourning gave light grey a ritual role. In Pastoureau's account of black, the clothing calendar for a death moved from black to purple, called half-mourning, and then to light gray, called quarter-mourning [4]. He adds that this strict color coding only became common in the nineteenth century [4].

In painting, Pastoureau argues that Vermeer's palette depends on grays, light gray above all, for the harmony of his pictures [5]. Gurney notes that under overcast light a sky often reads as light gray or white, and is usually the lightest note in the painting [6]. Linen shows the same pale grey in cloth: left natural, it ranges from off-white through brown or light gray[7].

sections.title: A grey that changes with its neighbors
sections.body:
Albers uses light grey as his example of an unstable color. A light grey can look dark at one moment and almost white at another, because how we see it is relative [8]. In one of his plates, a very light grey and a near-black grey are made to look alike by changing what surrounds them [9]. He also warns that poor reproductions push their greys to the extremes, leaving too few of the middle ones [8].

Livingstone makes the point from the other side. If the red and blue of a Lichtenstein cathedral are redrawn as light gray and black, the cathedral's shape appears at once, because the two now differ in lightness [10].

A related myth says that Le Corbusier's buildings were all white [11]. Batchelor reports that his Pavilion of the New Spirit was painted in ten colors, light grey among them, and that Wigley counts only one white building in his career [11]. The all-white legend is not true.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 796 works, 3.3 per cent [12]. It is almost always a highlight, playing that role in 98 per cent of the paintings that carry it [12]. Its nearest company in the archive is white, silver and ecru [12].

The biggest examples are pale all over. [[painter:claude-monet|Monet's]] [[painting:nga-45872|Morning Haze]] of 1888 reads as this grey across the whole photograph, and [[painter:piet-mondrian|Mondrian's]] [[painting:aic-65821|Composition Gray-Red]] of 1935 holds it over 90 per cent of the canvas [12]. It grows more common over time: 112 of 1,674 works in the 1900s, 6.7 per cent, with the 1920s at 17 of 237 [12]. Impressionism has it in 10 of 140 works, and [[painter:carlos-de-haes|Carlos de Haes]] in 12 of 29 [12]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [12].

The spelling matters too. In Google Books, *grey* peaks around 1865, and by 2000 it stands at about 39 per cent of that peak [13].
